lessons.title: Sector Rotation: Who Led Each Indian Market Era

body.text: Every Indian bull market has had a different set of heroes, and the heroes of one era have rarely led the next. The sectors everyone owns at the top of a cycle are usually the ones that disappoint for years afterwards.

children.text: The first two lessons of this chapter looked at commodity and interest rate cycles. Neither moves every stock equally. A rise in oil helps ONGC and hurts airlines. A rate cut helps NBFCs more than FMCG companies. As these cycles turn, money moves from one group of sectors to another, and market leadership changes. This is called sector rotation. This lesson explains why it happens, walks through who led each Indian market era, and shows why chasing last cycle's winners has been one of the most reliable ways to underperform.

body.caption: The forces that shift leadership from one sector to another

cells: Falling rates favour borrowers and long-duration growth stocks. Rising rates favour cash-rich, steady businesses
Rising commodity prices lift metals and energy producers and squeeze companies that buy those inputs
Capex booms lift capital goods, infrastructure, cement and banks lending to them. Capex busts sink the same group
A weak rupee boosts exporters such as IT services and pharma. A strong rupee helps importers and hurts exporters
Government priorities, such as infrastructure spending, bank recapitalisation or manufacturing incentives, create new winners
Leaders become expensive and crowded, so even good news stops lifting them, while neglected sectors become cheap enough to surprise on the upside

markDefs.definition: Sectors whose profits depend heavily on the state of the economy, such as banks, autos, real estate, metals and capital goods. Their earnings swing sharply between booms and slowdowns.
Sectors whose demand stays relatively steady through the economic cycle, such as FMCG, pharmaceuticals and utilities, because people keep buying essentials in good times and bad.

children.text: Textbooks, mostly based on US data, describe a classic rotation through the business cycle.
tend to lead when the economy is recovering and expanding, while

tend to hold up better when growth slows. Treat the model below as a starting framework, not a rulebook: real cycles are messier, and in India the rupee, government policy and foreign flows often override it.

body.caption: The classic business cycle rotation model (a rough guide, not a timing tool)

cells: Rates have been cut, growth is bottoming, sentiment is poor
Banks and NBFCs, autos, real estate, consumer discretionary
Growth is solid, credit is expanding, companies start investing
Capacity is tight, inflation and commodity prices rise, rates start going up
Growth falls, profits come under pressure, rates may start to be cut

children.text: Who Led Each Indian Market Era

events.title: ICE: information technology, communication, entertainment
events.description: The dot-com boom and Indian IT's Y2K success sent Infosys, Wipro, Satyam, Zee and a long tail of smaller tech names soaring. After the 2000 to 2001 bust, the leading IT services companies survived and grew, but many smaller ICE favourites collapsed and never recovered.

events.title: Infrastructure, capital goods, power, real estate and metals
events.description: The capex and commodity supercycle of Lesson 3.3 made L&T, BHEL, power developers, real estate companies such as DLF and Unitech, and steelmakers the market's leaders. IT services lagged in 2007 as the rupee strengthened to around 39 per dollar. FMCG looked boring.

events.title: FMCG, IT, pharma and private banks
events.description: In the long grind of Lesson 3.4, steady consumer companies such as Hindustan Unilever, ITC and Nestle India, IT exporters helped by a weak rupee, pharma exporters and cleaner private banks hit records. The 2007 leaders, infrastructure, real estate, power and public sector banks, slumped.

events.title: Private banks, NBFCs, consumer and mid caps
events.description: Falling inflation and rates, plus rising consumption, made private banks, NBFCs such as Bajaj Finance and consumer companies the big winners. Mid and small caps boomed in 2017 before a sharp fall in 2018. Pharma, a 2013 leader, fell for years on US pricing pressure and regulatory problems, and public sector banks struggled under bad loans.

events.title: IT, pharma, metals and the digital economy
events.description: The pandemic boosted IT services and pharma. Cheap money and a global commodity rebound lifted metals in 2021. New-age technology IPOs and small caps drew huge retail interest.

events.title: PSUs, defence, railways, power and capital goods
events.description: Government capex, cleaned-up public sector bank balance sheets, defence manufacturing and railway spending made PSU stocks, defence companies such as HAL and BEL, railway stocks, power utilities and capital goods the leaders. IT, new-age tech and some large private banks lagged for long stretches.

events.title: A reset
events.description: In the correction from September 2024, many of the hottest PSU, railway and small cap favourites fell far more than the Nifty, a familiar sign that a leadership phase was maturing. Who leads next is, as always, clearer in hindsight.

body.text: Notice the pattern of reversals. Infrastructure led in 2007 and was among the worst performers from 2010 to 2013, then led again in 2023. FMCG looked boring in 2007, led from 2009 to 2013, then lagged in the PSU rally. Pharma led in 2013, struggled until 2019, then bounced in 2020. Sectors do come back, but often only after a long wait, and not always with the same companies in charge.

body.title: The Cost of Chasing Last Cycle's Winner
body.prompt: A hot sector rises 200% in one market era, then falls 60% in the next. What is its total percentage gain across both eras combined?
body.explanation: ₹100 becomes ₹300 after a 200% rise, then ₹300 × 0.40 = ₹120 after a 60% fall. Total gain: 20%. Compare a boring sector that rises 50% and then 20%: ₹100 becomes ₹150, then ₹180, a total gain of 80%. An investor who bought the hot sector at the start of the second era would have lost 60%, even though its combined record looks positive.

children.text: The Nifty 50 and Sensex are weighted by market value, so their composition quietly records each era's winners. Around 2008 the indices carried much heavier weights in energy, metals, capital goods, power and real estate than they do today, and companies such as DLF, Unitech, Suzlon Energy and Reliance Communications were index constituents. As those companies shrank, they were dropped and replaced by the next era's winners. Today financial services dominate the Nifty 50.

body.title: Nifty 50 sector weights, approximate, around mid 2025 (%)
Market-cap weighting and rotation: the good and the bad

columns.label: Why it helps index investors
points: The index automatically adds rising companies and drops shrinking ones
You never have to predict which sector leads next
Failed leaders, such as many 2008 real estate and power names, get removed without any decision from you
Costs stay low because there is no active sector switching

columns.label: Where it can hurt
points: Weights rise most in whatever has already risen most, so the index is heaviest in recent winners near a peak
A single dominant sector, like financials today, can drive a large share of index returns
Stocks are often added after their big gains and removed after their big losses
It does not protect you from a rotation away from the sector that dominates the index

body.title: Test Yourself
body.question: The rupee weakens sharply over a year while domestic interest rates are rising and government infrastructure spending is being cut. Based on this lesson, which sector is most likely to hold up relatively well?
options: IT services exporters earning in dollars
NBFCs that depend on borrowing to lend
body.explanation: A weaker rupee raises the rupee value of dollar revenues for IT exporters, and they typically carry little debt, so rising rates hurt them less. Real estate developers and NBFCs suffer from higher borrowing costs, and infrastructure companies suffer when government spending is cut. This is roughly the setting of 2013, when IT exporters did well while infrastructure and real estate struggled.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: During the 1999 to 2000 technology boom, Indian market favourites in information technology, communication and entertainment were known as ___ stocks.
body.explanation: ICE stood for information technology, communication and entertainment. Like railway shares in the 1840s and infrastructure stocks in 2007, the label captured a real long-term trend and a price bubble at the same time.

body.text: Thematic fund launches are one of the clearest signs that a sector is crowded. When several fund houses launch new funds focused on the same hot theme, such as infrastructure in 2007 or PSU, defence and manufacturing funds in 2023 and 2024, they are responding to investor demand created by past returns. New thematic funds tend to arrive near the peak of a theme's popularity, not at the start.

body.title: Is This Sector Crowded?
steps: Is the sector trading well above its own historical average P/E or price to book value on screener.in or niftyindices.com?
Has its weight in the Nifty 50 or in popular funds risen sharply in the last two or three years?
Are fund houses launching new thematic funds focused on it?
Do analysts, news channels and friends all agree it is the obvious place to be?
Are earnings still growing faster than expected, or are share prices now running ahead of earnings?
Has the sector started to fall more than the index during market dips, a sign that crowded holders are selling first?

body.title: The PSU Portfolio
body.scenario: It is mid 2024. Your cousin in Hyderabad has watched PSU banks, defence, railway and power stocks lead the market for two years. She has sold her IT and FMCG holdings, which she calls "dead money", and now holds almost entirely PSU, defence and railway stocks plus two thematic funds in the same space. Her portfolio is up strongly and she feels the story has years to run.
body.prompt: Using the history of sector rotation in India, what would you point out, and what would you suggest?
body.modelAnswer: Her themes have real substance: government capex, cleaner public sector bank balance sheets and a defence manufacturing push genuinely lifted profits. But her portfolio now looks like an infrastructure-heavy portfolio in 2007 or an FMCG-heavy portfolio in 2013: concentrated in the last era's winners after a huge run, with valuations well above their own history and new thematic funds launching in the same space, both crowding signals. History shows leaders rarely lead the next era, and they often fall hardest when the market corrects, which is what happened to many of these stocks from late 2024. Meanwhile the sectors she sold as dead money, IT and FMCG, are exactly the kind of neglected groups that have led at other points, as FMCG did after 2008 and IT did in 2020. Nobody can time the rotation precisely, and her themes may still do well. A cycle-aware approach would be to decide on a target allocation across sectors, perhaps using a diversified index fund as the core, take some profits from the crowded themes to bring them back to that target, and rebalance periodically rather than letting the latest winners grow into most of her portfolio.

cards.definition: The movement of money and market leadership from one group of sectors to another as economic, commodity, rate and policy cycles change.
Sectors whose earnings swing with the economy, such as banks, autos, real estate, metals and capital goods.
Sectors with relatively steady demand through the cycle, such as FMCG, pharma and utilities.
Information technology, communication and entertainment stocks that led India's 1999 to 2000 tech boom.
A sector or theme so widely owned and popular that few new buyers remain, making it vulnerable to sharp falls when sentiment changes.
Periodically selling some of what has risen and adding to what has lagged, to bring a portfolio back to its target allocation.

body.label: Nifty Indices: Sectoral Indices
body.description: NSE's index website publishes factsheets and historical data for sector indices such as Nifty Bank, Nifty IT, Nifty FMCG, Nifty Pharma, Nifty Metal, Nifty Realty and Nifty PSU Bank, including their P/E and weights. Compare their returns over different eras to see rotation for yourself.

children.text: Commodities, rates and sector rotation are the cycles underneath the index. Chapter 5 brings the course together and asks the practical question: how do you use all this history without being fooled by it? It starts with the most useful single measure of where a market sits in its cycle, valuations at tops and bottoms.

body.text: Sector and company references in this lesson describe broad historical trends for education only, and dates of leadership phases are approximate. Index weights change regularly, so check the latest NSE factsheet. Nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell any security, sector or fund, or investment advice.

points: Sector leadership rotates as interest rates, commodities, the investment cycle, the rupee, policy and valuations change
The classic model has cyclicals leading in recoveries and expansions and defensives holding up in slowdowns, but in India the rupee, policy and foreign flows often override it

India's leaders changed almost every era: ICE stocks in 1999 to 2000, infrastructure and real estate in 2003 to 2008, FMCG, IT and pharma in 2009 to 2013, private banks and NBFCs in 2014 to 2019, and PSUs, defence and railways in 2022 to 2024
Leaders of one era rarely lead the next, and a sector that rises 200% then falls 60% ends up only 20% higher
Market-cap weighted indices rotate automatically by adding winners and dropping losers, but they are also heaviest in recent winners near peaks
Crowding signals include valuations far above history, rising index weights, analyst unanimity and a wave of thematic fund launches
